items.stem: Which of these is an ELEMENT of design (a building block), not a principle?
items.explanation: Elements are the raw ingredients: point, line, shape, form, space, colour, value and texture. Principles (balance, contrast, emphasis, rhythm, unity, proportion) describe how those ingredients are arranged.

distractors.c: Balance is a principle: how elements are arranged.
distractors.d: Emphasis is a principle that creates a focal point.
distractors.a: Rhythm is a principle created by repetition.

items.stem: The difference between 'shape' and 'form' in design is that…

options.text: Shape is coloured; form is not
Shape is two-dimensional; form is three-dimensional
Shape is curved; form is straight

items.explanation: A circle is a shape; a sphere is a form. Shading, perspective and overlap turn shapes into forms on paper.

distractors.d: Both can be curved or straight.

items.stem: The empty area around and between objects in a design is called…
items.explanation: Negative space gives objects room to breathe and can form shapes of its own; the FedEx logo hides an arrow between the E and x.

distractors.a: Positive space is the area the objects themselves occupy.

items.takeaway: Design the gaps, not just the things.

items.stem: Which element describes how light or dark a colour is?
items.explanation: Value is lightness/darkness. Strong value contrast keeps a design readable even in black and white.

distractors.d: Hue is the colour family, like red or blue.
distractors.b: Line is a mark between two points.

items.stem: A poster where one big red circle stands out among small grey squares mainly uses…
items.explanation: Making one element different in colour, size and shape creates a focal point: contrast in service of emphasis.

distractors.a: The grey squares repeat, but the point is the circle standing out.
distractors.b: Nothing here depends on mirror symmetry.

items.takeaway: Break the pattern to create a focal point.

items.stem: Asymmetrical balance is achieved when…

options.text: All elements are the same size
Unequal elements on either side feel equally weighted

items.explanation: A large light shape can balance a small dark one; a big object near the centre can balance a small one near the edge. It feels dynamic yet stable.

items.stem: A rangoli or a mandala usually shows which type of balance?
items.explanation: Elements radiating evenly from a central point create radial balance, also seen in wheels, flowers and clock faces.

distractors.b: Rangoli patterns repeat evenly around a centre.
distractors.d: They repeat in many directions, not just left-right.

items.stem: 'Visual hierarchy' in a layout refers to…

options.text: The order in which the eye reads elements, from most to least important
Placing the logo at the top

items.explanation: Size, weight, colour, contrast and position tell the viewer what to read first, second and third. Without hierarchy, everything competes and nothing is read.

distractors.b: Colour can create hierarchy, but hierarchy is about reading order.
distractors.c: That's one possible choice, not the definition.

items.takeaway: Decide reading order: 1 big, 2–3 medium, rest small.

items.stem: Rows of identical windows on a building create…
items.explanation: Repeating similar elements at regular intervals creates rhythm, which the eye follows like a beat in music.

distractors.a: Nothing stands out; they're all the same.
distractors.b: They're in rows, not around a centre.
distractors.c: Identical windows have little contrast with each other.

items.stem: Which principle is most violated by a shop board where every word is the same size and colour?
items.explanation: When everything is equally loud, nothing is heard. The shop name or product should dominate; details should be smaller.

items.stem: The golden ratio is approximately…
items.explanation: The golden ratio (≈1.618) appears in nature and classical art and architecture, and is used for pleasing proportions. A-series paper uses √2 (≈1.414) so halving keeps the same shape.

distractors.c: That's √2, the ratio of A-series paper.

items.stem: A4 paper folded in half gives A5 with the same proportions. This works because the ratio of the sides is…
items.explanation: Only a √2 rectangle keeps its proportions when halved. That's why A-series sizes (A0 → A1 → A2…) scale neatly.

distractors.d: Halving a golden rectangle doesn't keep its proportions.
distractors.a: Halving a 2:1 sheet gives a square.

items.stem: 'Unity' in a design means…

options.text: All parts look like they belong together

items.explanation: Unity comes from consistency in colour, type, shape language and spacing, so the design reads as one whole rather than a collection.

items.stem: We see a dotted outline of a circle as a complete circle. Which Gestalt principle is this?
items.explanation: Our brain fills gaps to complete familiar shapes. Many logos (IBM's striped letters, the WWF panda) depend on closure.

distractors.a: Proximity groups things that are close together.
distractors.b: Similarity groups things that look alike.

items.stem: Buttons placed close together on a remote are understood as one group. This is…
items.explanation: Things close to each other are seen as related. Designers group related controls and separate unrelated ones with space.

distractors.c: Common fate is about things moving together.

items.stem: The famous 'vase or two faces' picture demonstrates…
items.explanation: The image can be read as a vase (figure) on a background, or two faces with the vase as background. Figure–ground lets designers hide second images in negative space.

distractors.b: Proximity is about distance between elements.
distractors.c: Repetition is a design principle, not this effect.

items.takeaway: What's object and what's background can flip.

items.stem: In a chart, all the red dots are read as one group even though they're scattered. Which principle?
items.explanation: Elements that share colour, shape or size are perceived as related. That's why consistent colour coding works.

items.stem: The eye follows a smooth curve through a cluster of shapes rather than jumping at sharp angles. This is…
items.explanation: We prefer smooth, continuous paths. Designers use curves and lines to guide the eye through a layout.

distractors.a: Closure completes gaps in a shape.

items.stem: 'Form follows function' means that…

options.text: Decoration is more important than use
An object's shape should come from what it needs to do

items.explanation: The phrase, associated with architect Louis Sullivan, guided modernist design: purpose first, then form that serves it.

items.stem: Why do many kettle handles have a gap between handle and body?

options.text: To make it lighter to pour
To keep hands away from the hot surface

items.explanation: Heat insulation and knuckle clearance are classic form-follows-function decisions.

distractors.d: The gap is for safety and comfort, not saving material.

items.takeaway: Touch points need heat and clearance thinking.

items.stem: A stainless-steel tumbler is slightly narrower at the bottom than at the top. The main reason is…

options.text: So tumblers can be stacked inside each other

items.explanation: A tapered form nests, saving shelf space in homes, hotels and canteens. Many stackable objects (cups, chairs, buckets) are tapered.

items.stem: In Don Norman's terms, a flat metal plate on a door 'says' push. This cue is called a…
items.explanation: Signifiers communicate how to use something. A plate signals push; a handle signals pull. 'The Design of Everyday Things' popularised the term.

distractors.a: Feedback tells you an action worked.

items.stem: A lift button lights up when pressed. This is an example of…
items.explanation: Feedback tells the user their action was received, which prevents repeated pressing and uncertainty.

distractors.c: Affordance is what an object allows you to do.

items.stem: A USB-C plug that works either way up removes the need to check orientation. This design reduces…

options.text: Errors and frustration through forgiving design

items.explanation: Designing so that mistakes can't happen (or don't matter) is better than warning people about them.

distractors.d: Mapping is about controls and their effects.

items.stem: Stove knobs arranged in the same layout as the burners they control show good…
items.explanation: Natural mapping makes the relationship between controls and results obvious, so no labels are needed.

distractors.c: Signifiers show how to use something.

items.takeaway: Lay out controls like what they control.

items.stem: Which is the BEST sign that a product is poorly designed?

options.text: Users need written instructions stuck on it to use it correctly

items.explanation: If people need a note saying 'PUSH' or 'Switch 3 = fan', the design itself isn't communicating.

distractors.b: Material alone doesn't make design bad.

items.takeaway: Labels on labels mean a design failed.

items.stem: Anthropometry is the study of…
items.explanation: Designers use anthropometric data (heights, reach, grip sizes) to size furniture, tools and spaces for real people.

items.stem: When designing a public bus grab-rail height, designers usually aim to fit…

options.text: A wide range of users, e.g. from the 5th to the 95th percentile

items.explanation: Designing for a range (often 5th–95th percentile, plus extra options like lower rails) includes most people. Designing for an 'average' fits almost nobody well.

items.stem: Which chair feature most helps someone sitting for a 3-hour exam?

options.text: Lower-back (lumbar) support and the right seat height

items.explanation: Supporting the lower back's natural curve and letting feet rest flat reduces fatigue over long periods.

distractors.d: A flat hard back doesn't support the spine's curve.

items.stem: Why are many cutting tools for elderly users made with thicker, softer handles?

options.text: A thicker, cushioned grip needs less finger strength and reduces pain

items.explanation: Larger diameters spread force and suit weaker or arthritic hands, which is inclusive design benefiting everyone.
items.takeaway: Bigger, softer grips need less force.

items.stem: The rule of thirds suggests placing key elements…

options.text: Along the lines dividing the frame into thirds

items.explanation: A 3×3 grid's lines and intersections are strong positions that usually feel more dynamic than the centre.

items.stem: A doorway around a person in a photo, focusing attention on them, is called…
items.explanation: Natural frames (doors, windows, arches) isolate the subject and add depth.

distractors.b: Leading lines guide the eye along lines.
distractors.d: That's empty area around a subject.

items.takeaway: Use the scene to frame the subject.

items.stem: A layout grid in a magazine mainly helps by…

options.text: Creating consistent alignment and spacing across pages

items.explanation: Grids bring order: columns, margins and gutters keep layouts consistent, readable and fast to design.

items.stem: A typeface with small strokes at the ends of letters is called…
items.explanation: Serifs (like Times New Roman) feel traditional and bookish; sans-serifs (like Helvetica) feel clean and modern.

items.stem: For a railway station sign read from far away, which typeface choice is generally best?

options.text: A clear sans-serif with generous spacing

items.explanation: Simple, open letterforms with good spacing and high contrast stay legible at distance and speed.

distractors.d: Scripts are hard to read at distance.
distractors.b: Condensed letters blur together at distance.

items.stem: The space between lines of text is called…
items.explanation: Leading (pronounced 'ledding') comes from strips of lead placed between lines of metal type. Too little feels cramped; too much breaks paragraphs apart.

distractors.c: Kerning is space between specific letter pairs.
distractors.a: The baseline is the line letters sit on.

items.stem: Adjusting the space between two specific letters, like 'A' and 'V', is called…
items.explanation: Kerning fixes awkward gaps between certain letter pairs, important in logos and headlines.

items.stem: Which makes a headline stand out MOST in a text-heavy poster?

options.text: Large size and heavy weight with space around it

items.explanation: Hierarchy comes from contrast: size, weight and space. Isolate the headline and make it clearly different.

distractors.c: If everything is bold, nothing stands out.

items.stem: Pictograms used at international airports work well mainly because they…

options.text: Communicate without depending on one language

items.explanation: Simple, consistent pictograms cross language barriers, crucial in a multilingual country like India.

items.stem: The influential sports pictograms for the 1972 Munich Olympics were designed by…
items.explanation: Aicher built the pictograms on a strict grid with lines at fixed angles, setting a model for later systems.

distractors.b: Paul Rand designed corporate logos like IBM.

items.stem: A good set of pictograms (e.g. for a hospital) should share…

options.text: The same line weight, style and grid
Different styles to stand out from each other

items.explanation: Consistency makes a set read as one system, so people learn it once and recognise it everywhere.

distractors.b: Mixed styles look chaotic and confuse users.
distractors.d: Detail reduces clarity at small sizes.

items.stem: A logo made only of the company's name in a special typeface is called a…
items.explanation: Wordmarks (e.g. Google, Coca-Cola) rely on distinctive lettering.

distractors.b: An emblem encloses text in a badge or shape.
distractors.c: A pictorial mark is an image.

items.takeaway: Wordmark = the name as the logo.

items.stem: Which quality matters MOST for a logo that will appear on app icons and on large hoardings?

options.text: It works at very small and very large sizes, in one colour

items.explanation: Scalability and one-colour reproduction are core tests of a strong logo.
items.takeaway: Test logos tiny and in black.

items.stem: The 'I ♥ NY' logo is a famous example of…

options.text: Using a symbol to replace a word

items.explanation: Milton Glaser replaced 'love' with a heart: instantly readable across languages and endlessly copied.

distractors.c: It uses type and a symbol.

items.takeaway: A symbol can stand in for a word.

items.stem: The main functions of packaging include all EXCEPT…

options.text: Making it easy to carry and store
Making the product heavier so it seems valuable

items.explanation: Packaging protects, contains, informs, sells and should be easy to dispose of. Adding weight only adds waste and transport cost.

items.stem: Why are kulhads (unglazed clay cups) considered sustainable?

options.text: They are made of local clay and break down back into soil

items.explanation: Kulhads use local material and labour and return to the earth, though firing uses energy and fertile topsoil, so they aren't perfect.

items.stem: 'Slack fill' in packaging means…

options.text: Packages with much more empty space than product

items.explanation: Slack fill misleads buyers and wastes material, a common complaint with chips packets.

items.stem: In India, a triangular road sign with a red border usually gives a…
items.explanation: Shape encodes message type: triangle = caution, circle = rule, rectangle = information.

items.stem: Where should a wayfinding sign be placed to be MOST useful?

options.text: At the very end of a corridor
At decision points, where people must choose a direction

items.explanation: Wayfinding works when information appears exactly where a decision is needed, at eye level.

distractors.a: By then the choice is made.
distractors.b: Too high is hard to notice.
distractors.c: People need help along the way.

items.stem: A hospital uses coloured lines on the floor leading to different departments. This is an example of…

options.text: Wayfinding through colour coding and continuity

items.explanation: Floor lines are easy to follow for anxious or non-reading visitors: a simple, inclusive wayfinding system.

distractors.a: The lines have a clear function.

items.stem: Why do many Indian signs show text in two or three scripts?

options.text: It's required on all private signs
To be readable by speakers of different languages

items.explanation: Multilingual signage is essential in India. Designers must balance multiple scripts while keeping hierarchy and legibility.

distractors.b: It's a communication choice, often required on public signs.

items.stem: A line that guides the viewer's eye towards the main subject is called…
items.explanation: Roads, rivers, rails and edges can lead the eye to the subject, a powerful composition tool.

distractors.b: Contour lines describe edges of forms.

items.stem: Making a child much smaller than a giant tree in an illustration mainly creates…
items.explanation: Contrast in scale tells a story about size and feeling: smallness, awe, vulnerability.

items.stem: Which arrangement feels most stable and calm?

options.text: A wide, symmetrical composition with strong horizontals

items.explanation: Horizontals and symmetry suggest rest; diagonals suggest movement; crowding suggests tension.

items.stem: Leaving large empty space around a single object in a poster usually makes the object feel…
items.explanation: Negative space isolates and elevates the subject, which premium brands often use.

items.stem: Why do public-park benches often have armrests in the middle?

options.text: To help people stand up, and to divide seating space

items.explanation: Middle armrests help elderly people push themselves up and define personal space. Critics note they are sometimes added to stop people sleeping, which raises an ethical question about 'hostile' design.
items.takeaway: Every feature has users, and sometimes victims.

items.stem: 'Hostile architecture' refers to…

options.text: Design features meant to stop certain uses, like spikes preventing people from sitting

items.explanation: Spikes on ledges or sloped benches exclude homeless people and others. Designers must consider who a design excludes.
items.takeaway: Ask who a design pushes away.

items.stem: A computer screen's top edge should ideally be…

options.text: At or slightly below eye level

items.explanation: A screen at or just below eye level keeps the neck neutral during long work.

items.stem: The moulded paper-pulp trays used for eggs are usually made from…
items.explanation: Moulded pulp is cheap, shock-absorbing, compostable and made from waste paper: a classic sustainable package.

items.stem: Which is generally EASIEST to read in long paragraphs on paper?

options.text: Sentence case in a regular-weight text face

items.explanation: Lower-case words have distinctive shapes that help fast reading; all caps and heavy styling slow it down.

distractors.c: All caps slow reading because word shapes disappear.

items.stem: When testing a new pictogram, the most useful question is…

options.text: Can people unfamiliar with it guess its meaning quickly?

items.explanation: Comprehension testing with real users (including non-readers and visitors) is the best check.

items.stem: Why might a company 'flatten' its logo (removing 3D effects and gradients)?

options.text: Flat designs reproduce clearly on screens, small icons and print
Flat logos are always cheaper to print

items.explanation: Simplified logos stay crisp across app icons, favicons, embroidery and single-colour printing.

items.stem: An exit sign is usually green with a running figure because…

options.text: Green signals safety and the figure communicates without words

items.explanation: International safety signs use green for safe conditions and exits, and pictograms that work for everyone in an emergency.

items.stem: Many water bottles for cyclists have a squeezable body and a push-pull valve. The design priority here is…

options.text: Drinking quickly with one hand while moving

items.explanation: The user's context (riding, one hand free) determines the form: soft body, quick valve, grippy shape.

items.stem: A switchboard with ten identical unlabelled switches mostly lacks…
items.explanation: Users can't tell which switch controls what. Grouping by area, icons or layout matching the room would fix it.

items.stem: Lever-style door handles are recommended over round knobs in inclusive design because they…

options.text: Can be operated with an elbow or a closed fist, no grip needed

items.explanation: Round knobs need grip and twist, hard for arthritic hands, children or someone carrying bags. Levers work for almost everyone.

items.stem: In a storyboard frame, the 'establishing shot' is usually a…

options.text: Wide shot showing where the scene takes place

items.explanation: Films and storyboards often open with a wide shot to orient the viewer before moving closer.

items.stem: Which element is created when a surface looks rough, smooth or bumpy in a drawing?
items.explanation: Visual texture is suggested by mark-making; tactile texture is physical.

items.stem: In a group of identical blue chairs, one red chair stands out. The red chair becomes the…
items.explanation: Breaking a pattern with one different element creates an instant focal point.

distractors.c: The blue chairs form the rhythm.

items.stem: Birds flying in the same direction are perceived as one flock. This is the Gestalt principle of…
items.explanation: Elements moving in the same direction are perceived as a group, useful in animation and interface motion.

items.stem: Which colour combination gives the highest legibility for a sign?
items.explanation: High value contrast matters most. Black on yellow is among the most legible combinations, which is why it's used for warnings.

distractors.b: Low value contrast and problematic for colour blindness.

items.stem: Which packaging change would MOST reduce waste for a spice brand?

options.text: Refillable containers with paper refill pouches
Using multi-layer foil for each spoonful
Making the jar larger with the same amount inside

items.explanation: Refill systems reuse the durable container and minimise disposable material.
